ED 3330 - Children’s Literature
Credits: 4
An introduction to the study of literature for children in the pre‑school and elementary grades. The course includes,
selection and evaluation of books for children; language development through children’s literature; use of literature to
promote the social, emotional and creative development of children; integrating children’s literature into the content
areas; planning story activities. Opportunities to work with children ages 3‑7 where feasible.
Prerequisites
EC1; EC II Recommended: ED 3700 - Child Development
as prerequisite or co-requisite
When Offered:
Occasionally.
ED 3700 - Child Development
Credits: 4
Provides students with background information concerning the intellectual, physiological, social, emotional, and
creative development of children from birth through the elementary school years. Emphasis is given to the contributions
of Piaget, Gardner and other developmental theorists. Practical relevance of child development information is stressed
throughout this course for students who plan to work with children. Students will participate in a practicum in a field-
based classroom to gain experience with children in an educational setting and to reflect upon teaching as a career.
Prerequisites

ED 3742 - Middle Childhood and Adolescence
Credits: 4
Examines human development from six years through adolescence. Research and theories concerning physical,
cognitive, personality and social development will be reviewed. Family, peer groups, schools and media will be
discussed. The impact of socioeconomic background, culture, race and gender will be discussed throughout. The use of
theories and research in applied settings will be discussed.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every semester.
ED 3800 - Human Development and Learning
Credits: 4
This course focuses on the development of learners from birth through adolescence, their phases of learning, their
intellectual, social, and emotional growth, character development, individual differences, interests, attention, potential
challenges, and motivation. Candidates will examine how these aspects of human development relate and influence the
teaching and learning process. 15 hours of field experience required.

ED 3900 - Foundations of Education
Credits: 4
This course will offer an introduction to the world of teaching, as it examines the basic theories of learning and teaching
across educational environments for the birth-12 learner. Specifically, the course encourages deeper understanding of the
educator and student in relation to others; it engages in an exploration of the social/historical/political contexts that
affect education and teaching; the significant characteristics that diverse student populations bring to the classroom; and
the related issues of curriculum and pedagogy across the lifespan. Over the course and cumulatively, we consider what
it means to be a reflective educator.

ED 4082 - Methods and Materials of Teaching Mathematics
Credits: 4
This course is a study of the strategies, techniques, materials, and technology used to teach mathematics to middle
childhood and high school students. Candidates will become acquainted with New York State learning standards
involved in teaching mathematics at the secondary school level, develop an awareness of the professional environment,
and of resources and information available for teachers. There will be a strong focus on unit and lesson planning,
assessment methods, interdisciplinary connections and differentiated instruction. The co-requisite Observation course
provides an opportunity for candidates to observe and interact with teachers and students in a secondary field
placement setting, and to reflect on these experiences.

and ED 3820

This course explores reading and writing in discipline-specific areas including English Language Arts, Science, Social
Studies, and Mathematics for students in the upper elementary grades (3-6). The course places a strong emphasis on
disciplinary and interdisciplinary uses and purposes for oral and written texts and includes research-based models for
integrating reading and writing across the curriculum. To support the goal of student comprehension, the course
emphasizes: (1) various forms of assessment to measure progress and plan instruction, (2) supporting vocabulary
acquisition through word work, (3) the use of strategy-based and interactive methods and materials for the upper
elementary classroom, and (4) the implementation of multiple texts to support instruction in English Language Arts and
in other disciplines.

ED 4221 - Teaching Literacy in Multilingual Settings
Credits: 4
In this course, participants critically examine the underlying theories and research-based literacy teaching and
assessment practices for multilingual learners who are developing literacy in more than one language. Participants will
design literacy instruction across the curriculum for children in their first language and English as a new language for
students from birth through grade six guided by the research-based building blocks of literacy commonly referred to as
the Science of Reading. Through active engagement with multicultural and multilingual children’s literature
participants gain an understanding of the role of this literature in language and literacy development in children’s home
and new languages.

ED 4225 - Literacy for Diverse Learners
Credits: 4
This course is designed to help teachers develop an understanding of the theory, research, and practice of teaching
reading and writing in PreK-12th grade classrooms with an added emphasis on the intersection with special and
bilingual education. The main goals of the course are: to gain an understanding of how students develop as listeners,
speakers, readers, and writers-cognitively, socially, linguistically, culturally; become familiar with a variety of
instructional practices that support young literacy learners; and, develop a working knowledge of assessment-driven
literacy instruction. In addition, several critical topics and themes are foundational to the course: high leverage practices
for special education and multilingual learners; valuing cultural diversity; exploring genre and author studies; and,
developing literacy curricula for democratic classrooms. There are 15 fieldwork hours required as part of this course.
ED 4230 - Reading Across the Curriculum
Credits: 4
This course focuses on current approaches to literacy instruction across the curriculum. It is designed for secondary
teacher candidates, and addresses specific instructional strategies appropriate for the adolescent population. Emphasis
will be placed on theoretical models of reading, instructional strategies, assessment techniques, strategies specific to
multicultural and bilingual learners.

ED 4250 - Linguistics for Language Educators
Credits: 4
Linguistics for Language Educators focuses on building knowledge related to the ways in which languages work in
teaching and learning. This course will benefit language educators of all kinds including bilingual, world language (i.e.
Spanish Education at the elementary or secondary level), English-for-Speakers-of-Other-Languages (ESOL) and any
teacher in a mainstream or special education classrooms with students designed as English Learners (ELs). This course
covers theories of language acquisition and linguistic components of language and provides educators with
opportunities to explore how current theories and practices in the field of linguistics are relevant to second language
teaching and learning. The course provides an overview of theories of language acquisition, linguistics, sociolinguistic
and psycholinguistic analyses and how these pertain to language proficiency and academic achievement for students
learning language in U.S. schools. Course topics include phonology, morphology, syntax, pragmatics, semantics,
sociolinguistics, linguistic anthropology, language variation, language acquisition (first, additional, simultaneous in
more than one language), written language, language processing, nonverbal components of language and comparative
linguistics for English and Spanish

ED 4300 - Assessment, Evaluation, and Evidence-based Decision Making in Special
Education
Credits: 4
The purpose of ED 4300 is to provide pre-service teachers with skills needed to use assessment data to make diagnostic
and instructional decisions for students classified with disabilities from birth through 12th grade. Pre-service teachers
will learn how to determine students’ strengths and areas of need by monitoring student progress across disciplines and
settings, conducting error analyses, conducting norm and criterion-referenced assessments, and using assessment results
to develop Individualized Educational Programs (IEPs) and Individualized Family Service Plans (IFSPs). In addition,
pre-service teachers will understand Response to Intervention (RTI) and Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), and
determine students’ responses to individualized educational interventions and plans using data. The process and
purpose of evaluations and data collection leading to the 13 classifications and classification of Preschool Child with a
Disability will be explored, including collaboration with family and professionals. Teacher candidates will explore biases
and their influence on assessment connected to students’ socioeconomic and cultural differences. 10 hours of field
experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900
When Offered:
This course is offered every semester.
ED 4670 - Methods and Materials of Teaching English as a Second Language
Credits: 4
This course will prepare pre-service teachers to make connections between theory and methodology for the teaching of
English as a Second Language in bilingual classrooms. The course will emphasize the needs of English learners (ELs) in
academic instruction, with a focus on language and literacy integration throughout the curriculum, content-based ESL,
and reading and writing strategies for English language learners. The course will provide interactive exploration of
research-based ESL classroom practices. Field experience required.

ED 4810 - Positive Behavior Supports and Interventions for Students with Disabilities
Credits: 4
This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the theoretical foundations of both classroom
management and behavior, and focuses on a wide range of proactive and preventative approaches to supporting
positive student behavior. Additional course topics include the application of evidence-based approaches to addressing
challenging behaviors in Birth through Grade 12 classroom settings, including the collection & analysis of student
behavioral data, and the creation function-based behavioral interventions to engage and support students who exhibit
challenging behavior. The course involves a practicum experience in a class serving at least one student with emotional
or behavioral disorder. During their practicum experience, students conduct a functional behavioral analysis (FBA) and
implement a behavior intervention plan (BIP) to support a focal student’s challenging behavior. The overarching goal of
the course is to equip pre-service teachers with a variety of practical, evidence-based strategies that are effective in
promoting positive student behaviors and addressing challenging Birth through Grade 12 classroom behaviors and
situations. 10 hours of field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900, ED 4225, ED 4250, ED 4280, ED 4300ED 3820 - Foundations of Special Education

ED 4890 - Students with Neurodevelopmental Disabilities and Special Health Care
Needs
Credits: 4
This course is focused on the collaborative practices that enable individuals with neurodevelopmental disabilities and
other health care needs to reach their maximum potential and lead meaningful lives. It explores issues related to
assessment and treatment of children with, or at risk for neurodevelopmental disabilities and their families. Students
examine current and historical experiences of learners with developmental disabilities, and analyze different theoretical
underpinnings related to teaching this population of learners from birth through adolescence. Additional foci include:
early intervention, family partnerships, advocacy, evidence-based instructional practices, and transition planning, with a
special focus throughout the course on Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). 10 hours of field experience required.

records.title: Children’s Literature
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
An introduction to the study of literature for children in the pre‑school and elementary grades. The course includes,
selection and evaluation of books for children; language development through children’s literature; use of literature to
promote the social, emotional and creative development of children; integrating children’s literature into the content
areas; planning story activities. Opportunities to work with children ages 3‑7 where feasible.
Prerequisites
EC1; EC II Recommended: ED 3700 - Child Development
as prerequisite or co-requisite
When Offered:
Occasionally.

records.title: Child Development
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Provides students with background information concerning the intellectual, physiological, social, emotional, and
creative development of children from birth through the elementary school years. Emphasis is given to the contributions
of Piaget, Gardner and other developmental theorists. Practical relevance of child development information is stressed
throughout this course for students who plan to work with children. Students will participate in a practicum in a field-
based classroom to gain experience with children in an educational setting and to reflect upon teaching as a career.
Prerequisites

EC1; EC II
When Offered:
Each semester.

records.title: Middle Childhood and Adolescence
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Examines human development from six years through adolescence. Research and theories concerning physical,
cognitive, personality and social development will be reviewed. Family, peer groups, schools and media will be
discussed. The impact of socioeconomic background, culture, race and gender will be discussed throughout. The use of
theories and research in applied settings will be discussed.
Prerequisites
EC II
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Human Development and Learning
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course focuses on the development of learners from birth through adolescence, their phases of learning, their
intellectual, social, and emotional growth, character development, individual differences, interests, attention, potential
challenges, and motivation. Candidates will examine how these aspects of human development relate and influence the
teaching and learning process. 15 hours of field experience required.

records.title: Foundations of Special Education
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course offers an introductory overview of the field of special education across the lifespan, which includes the
investigation of the development, nature, causes and characteristics of young children and adolescents with special
needs. Consistent with the knowledge base of the field, the course is based on an interdisciplinary perspective. We will

review an extensive body of information that relates to five broad topics: history of the field, basic notions, current
trends, and exceptionality categories and instructional technology. Some of the basic notions include philosophical and
legal foundations, structure of the service delivery system, instructional approaches and technology, and work with
families. Current trends will focus on minority representation, inclusion, and standards. Additionally, this course will
engage candidate in curriculum development across disability categories with a focus on the integration of appropriate
instructional technology. Lastly, definitions, prevalence, causes, assessment, characteristics, educational and instructional
technology considerations for several exceptionalities, and international perspectives will be studied. 15 hours of field
experience required.
Prerequisites
English Comp I and II with a B or higher
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Foundations of Education
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course will offer an introduction to the world of teaching, as it examines the basic theories of learning and teaching
across educational environments for the birth-12 learner. Specifically, the course encourages deeper understanding of the
educator and student in relation to others; it engages in an exploration of the social/historical/political contexts that
affect education and teaching; the significant characteristics that diverse student populations bring to the classroom; and
the related issues of curriculum and pedagogy across the lifespan. Over the course and cumulatively, we consider what
it means to be a reflective educator.
Prerequisite/Corequisite
English Comp I - C grade or higher
English Comp II- C grade or higher
MA 1020 and/or 2nd Math course: MA 2000, 2050, 2010, 2080, 2090, MA 8998- C grade or higher

records.title: Grade C or higher
records.sourceText:
32 credits - Course is only open to Sophomore, Junior and Seniors.
3.0 GPA

When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Methods and Materials of Teaching Mathematics
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is a study of the strategies, techniques, materials, and technology used to teach mathematics to middle
childhood and high school students. Candidates will become acquainted with New York State learning standards
involved in teaching mathematics at the secondary school level, develop an awareness of the professional environment,
and of resources and information available for teachers. There will be a strong focus on unit and lesson planning,
assessment methods, interdisciplinary connections and differentiated instruction. The co-requisite Observation course
provides an opportunity for candidates to observe and interact with teachers and students in a secondary field
placement setting, and to reflect on these experiences.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE; ED 3900
and ED 3820
or ED 3742
When Offered:
Every Spring.

records.sourceText:

teaching Spanish at the secondary school level, develop an awareness of the professional environment, and resources

records.sourceText:

This course is a study of the strategies, techniques, materials, and technology used to teach science to middle childhood

teaching science at the secondary school level, develop an awareness of the professional environment, and resources and

This course is a study of the strategies, techniques, materials, and technology used to teach social studies to middle
childhood and high school students. Candidates will become acquainted with New York State learning standards

involved in teaching social studies at the secondary school level, develop an awareness of the profes sional environment,
and resources and information available for teachers. There will be a strong focus on unit and lesson planning,
assessment methods, interdisciplinary connections and differentiated instruction. The co-requisite Observation course

records.title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Elementary Science
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to develop pre-service teachers’ skills and abilities in teaching science to preschool and
elementary school learners through inquiry and investigations. Emphasis is placed on how children learn science, lesson
planning, assessment of students’ scientific reasoning, safety practices, issues of diversity, and application of technology
in relation to New York State and National Science Standards.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED3700, ED3900 and proficiency in mathematics; completion of laboratory science.
When Offered:
Fall
Spring

records.title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Elementary Math
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course is designed to introduce principles, methods, and materials for teaching mathematics to diverse learners in
an early childhood and elementary classrooms. Emphasis is placed on how children learn mathematics, teaching
through problem solving and children’s literature, using different modes of representation including technology to
develop relational understanding and procedural fluency, principles of effective mathematics teaching, and Standards
for Mathematical Practice. Participants will develop the core ideas and methods of learning, teaching, planning, and
assessment in relation to State and National Mathematics Standards. Perspectives of how children learn mathematics
and issues of diversity is discussed.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED3700, ED3900, MA 1020 and a second math course
When Offered:
fall
spring

records.title: Literacy for All Students
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course will examine theory, research, and practice of literacy learning and teaching. Special attention is given to the
theoretical reading models, developmental stages of literacy, literacy skills and strategies, literacy assessment, planning
for English Language Learners, and integration of learning and teaching standards. This course will include practical
applications of methods and materials used in class. A field component is required.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED 3700
, ED 3900

records.title: Language Arts in the Context of Childhood Education
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4

This course explores reading and writing in discipline-specific areas including English Language Arts, Science, Social
Studies, and Mathematics for students in the upper elementary grades (3-6). The course places a strong emphasis on
disciplinary and interdisciplinary uses and purposes for oral and written texts and includes research-based models for
integrating reading and writing across the curriculum. To support the goal of student comprehension, the course
emphasizes: (1) various forms of assessment to measure progress and plan instruction, (2) supporting vocabulary
acquisition through word work, (3) the use of strategy-based and interactive methods and materials for the upper
elementary classroom, and (4) the implementation of multiple texts to support instruction in English Language Arts and
in other disciplines.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED3700, ED3900, Co-requisite: CE 4200
When Offered:
Fall
Spring

records.title: Teaching Literacy in Multilingual Settings
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
In this course, participants critically examine the underlying theories and research-based literacy teaching and
assessment practices for multilingual learners who are developing literacy in more than one language. Participants will
design literacy instruction across the curriculum for children in their first language and English as a new language for
students from birth through grade six guided by the research-based building blocks of literacy commonly referred to as
the Science of Reading. Through active engagement with multicultural and multilingual children’s literature
participants gain an understanding of the role of this literature in language and literacy development in children’s home
and new languages.
Prerequisites
Admission into the School of Education; ED 3700; ED 3900

When Offered:
Fall
Spring

records.title: Literacy for Diverse Learners
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to help teachers develop an understanding of the theory, research, and practice of teaching
reading and writing in PreK-12th grade classrooms with an added emphasis on the intersection with special and
bilingual education. The main goals of the course are: to gain an understanding of how students develop as listeners,
speakers, readers, and writers-cognitively, socially, linguistically, culturally; become familiar with a variety of
instructional practices that support young literacy learners; and, develop a working knowledge of assessment-driven
literacy instruction. In addition, several critical topics and themes are foundational to the course: high leverage practices
for special education and multilingual learners; valuing cultural diversity; exploring genre and author studies; and,
developing literacy curricula for democratic classrooms. There are 15 fieldwork hours required as part of this course.

records.title: Reading Across the Curriculum
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course focuses on current approaches to literacy instruction across the curriculum. It is designed for secondary
teacher candidates, and addresses specific instructional strategies appropriate for the adolescent population. Emphasis
will be placed on theoretical models of reading, instructional strategies, assessment techniques, strategies specific to
multicultural and bilingual learners.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED 3900
Corequisite ED4231Prerequisite/Corequisite
ED4231, ED3900
When Offered:
Every semester.

records.title: Reading Across the Curriculum Practicum
records.sourceText:
Credits: 2
The purpose of this course is to provide adolescence and middle childhood education candidates with an opportunity to
observe literacy strategies in various discipline settings. The course goal is to familiarize candidates with differentiation
of instruction and methodology for diverse / multicultural populations. Candidates will also become familiar with the
strategic needs of learners with exceptionalities. Candidates will observe students in a bilingual and/or ESL classroom,
and maintain a reflective journal. Field experience is required.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE; ED 3900Corequisite ED4230Prerequisite/Corequisite
ED4230, ED3900

records.title: Linguistics for Language Educators
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
Linguistics for Language Educators focuses on building knowledge related to the ways in which languages work in
teaching and learning. This course will benefit language educators of all kinds including bilingual, world language (i.e.
Spanish Education at the elementary or secondary level), English-for-Speakers-of-Other-Languages (ESOL) and any
teacher in a mainstream or special education classrooms with students designed as English Learners (ELs). This course
covers theories of language acquisition and linguistic components of language and provides educators with
opportunities to explore how current theories and practices in the field of linguistics are relevant to second language
teaching and learning. The course provides an overview of theories of language acquisition, linguistics, sociolinguistic
and psycholinguistic analyses and how these pertain to language proficiency and academic achievement for students
learning language in U.S. schools. Course topics include phonology, morphology, syntax, pragmatics, semantics,
sociolinguistics, linguistic anthropology, language variation, language acquisition (first, additional, simultaneous in
more than one language), written language, language processing, nonverbal components of language and comparative
linguistics for English and Spanish
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED 3700
, ED 3900

records.title: Language Development and Instruction for Diverse Learners
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to prepare pre-service teachers for instruction in reading and writing for Birth through 12th-
grade students with a focus on students with exceptionalities. Teacher candidates will gain knowledge of pedagogical
theories for reading and writing development and evidence-based instructional strategies for students across disciplines
and settings. The development of language and learning will be explored, as well as a balanced and integrated language
arts curriculum, including collaboration with professionals. Additionally, this course will provide essential methods for
teaching and assessing reading and writing for Pre-K students through 12th grade with an understanding of the
influence of individual experiences and socio-cultural/political contexts on literacy learning and its assessment. 10
hours of field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900ED 3900 - Foundations of Education

records.title: Methods and Materials for Teaching Mathematics and Sciences to Diverse
records.sourceText:
Students
Credits: 4
In this course candidates will learn different methods and materials for teaching and modifying instruction in
mathematics, sciences, and technology for diverse students in Birth -12th grade classrooms. It will provide a forum for
the discussion of different issues associated with the field of learning disabilities and special education. More
specifically students will have the opportunity to examine a wide range of effective age-appropriate instructional
technology and accommodative strategies for teaching different areas of the curriculum including mathematics,
sciences, technology, and study skills. Students will also have the opportunity to present, discuss, question and
exchange ideas that will contribute to our overall understanding of teaching and learning, and at the same time will
further the discourse and dynamics in the field of education. In the process of learning about all these important topics
we will all reflect on our experiences as learners and use this valuable resource to inform us with technology-infused
teaching practice. Diagnostic, remedial, and evaluative strategies will also be examined, as well as methods of
instruction aligned with the New York State Learning Standards and adapted for diverse student

populations. Additionally, the course is structured to enhance the development of critical thinking, and problem solving
with an emphasis on how technology can be used to increase student achievement and engagement to develop the
teacher-as-practitioner. 10 hours of field experience required.

records.title: Assessment, Evaluation, and Evidence-based Decision Making in Special
records.sourceText:
Education
Credits: 4
The purpose of ED 4300 is to provide pre-service teachers with skills needed to use assessment data to make diagnostic
and instructional decisions for students classified with disabilities from birth through 12th grade. Pre-service teachers
will learn how to determine students’ strengths and areas of need by monitoring student progress across disciplines and
settings, conducting error analyses, conducting norm and criterion-referenced assessments, and using assessment results
to develop Individualized Educational Programs (IEPs) and Individualized Family Service Plans (IFSPs). In addition,
pre-service teachers will understand Response to Intervention (RTI) and Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS), and
determine students’ responses to individualized educational interventions and plans using data. The process and
purpose of evaluations and data collection leading to the 13 classifications and classification of Preschool Child with a
Disability will be explored, including collaboration with family and professionals. Teacher candidates will explore biases
and their influence on assessment connected to students’ socioeconomic and cultural differences. 10 hours of field
experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900
When Offered:
This course is offered every semester.

records.title: Methods and Materials of Teaching English as a Second Language
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course will prepare pre-service teachers to make connections between theory and methodology for the teaching of
English as a Second Language in bilingual classrooms. The course will emphasize the needs of English learners (ELs) in
academic instruction, with a focus on language and literacy integration throughout the curriculum, content-based ESL,
and reading and writing strategies for English language learners. The course will provide interactive exploration of
research-based ESL classroom practices. Field experience required.

Prerequisites
ED3800, ED3900, ED3820

records.title: Positive Behavior Supports and Interventions for Students with Disabilities
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the theoretical foundations of both classroom
management and behavior, and focuses on a wide range of proactive and preventative approaches to supporting
positive student behavior. Additional course topics include the application of evidence-based approaches to addressing
challenging behaviors in Birth through Grade 12 classroom settings, including the collection & analysis of student
behavioral data, and the creation function-based behavioral interventions to engage and support students who exhibit
challenging behavior. The course involves a practicum experience in a class serving at least one student with emotional
or behavioral disorder. During their practicum experience, students conduct a functional behavioral analysis (FBA) and
implement a behavior intervention plan (BIP) to support a focal student’s challenging behavior. The overarching goal of
the course is to equip pre-service teachers with a variety of practical, evidence-based strategies that are effective in
promoting positive student behaviors and addressing challenging Birth through Grade 12 classroom behaviors and
situations. 10 hours of field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900, ED 4225, ED 4250, ED 4280, ED 4300ED 3820 - Foundations of Special Education
When Offered:
This course is offered every semester.

records.title: Instructional Design & Delivery for Diverse Learners
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The purpose of this course is to provide pre-service teachers with conceptual and application knowledge of instructional
design and delivery in English Language Arts and Social Studies for students with exceptionalities and all learners.
Focus will also be placed on students’ areas of strengths and needs, and how these inform the choice and application of
instructional methods such as scaffolds, differentiation, and Universal Design for Learning for learners. This course will

also cover research-based instructional strategies and skills and their implementation for enrichment and remediation
for students classified with disabilities across disciplines and settings to include inclusion and self-contained/special
classes. Preservice teachers will acquire an understanding of pedagogical strategies for students with disabilities from
birth through grade 12 and their connection to students’ socioeconomic and cultural diversity. This course is required for
all Exceptional Education and Learning majors. 10 hours of field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900, ED 4225, ED 4250, ED 4280, ED 4300ED 3820 - Foundations of Special Education

records.title: Students with Neurodevelopmental Disabilities and Special Health Care
records.sourceText:
Needs
Credits: 4
This course is focused on the collaborative practices that enable individuals with neurodevelopmental disabilities and
other health care needs to reach their maximum potential and lead meaningful lives. It explores issues related to
assessment and treatment of children with, or at risk for neurodevelopmental disabilities and their families. Students
examine current and historical experiences of learners with developmental disabilities, and analyze different theoretical
underpinnings related to teaching this population of learners from birth through adolescence. Additional foci include:
early intervention, family partnerships, advocacy, evidence-based instructional practices, and transition planning, with a
special focus throughout the course on Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). 10 hours of field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED 3800, ED 3820, ED 3900, ED 4225, ED 4250, ED 4280, ED 4300
When Offered:
This course is offered every semester

records.title: Spanish and Methods of Teaching in the Content Areas for Bilingual Teachers
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course intends to provide pre-service teachers with opportunities to listen, speak, read and write Spanish in the
academic contexts of the different content areas. The academic language necessary to teach in each content area will be
practiced within the exploration and discussion of best practices and methods to teach content in a bilingual classroom.

Bilingual children’s literature will be introduced and used throughout the course. Active participation in both
preparation for class and in-class discussions will aid in the development of the language skills needed to effectively
teach lessons in Spanish. Pre-service bilingual teachers will improve various aspects of Spanish writing including
grammar, phonetics, spelling, composition, and vocabulary in the context of the topics addressed in this course. Field
experience required.
Prerequisites

records.title: Child Development
Observation, Practicum, and Seminar
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course provides an opportunity for middle childhood and adolescence education majors to experience the school
environment prior to student teaching. Candidates spend 100 hours in schools for the purpose of observation of
instruction and other school activities, interaction with children and teachers, and reflection. This course is taken in
conjunction with a Methods in Teaching course, and is conducted under the supervision of a university supervisor.
Students participate in a weekly seminar.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, formal application required, ED3900Prerequisite/Corequisite
ED3900
When Offered:
Spring Semester

records.title: Student Teaching in Secondary School and Seminar (Grades 7-12)
records.sourceText:
Credits: 12
This is the capstone student teaching experience for candidates seeking certification in adolescence education in biology,
chemistry, mathematics, social studies and Spanish. This course provides an opportunity for candidates to apply
knowledge and skills developed in coursework under the guidance of a university supervisor and cooperating teacher.
This course is a full-time commitment, with half the semester spent at grades 7-9 and half at grades 10-12. Students

participate in a weekly seminar.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, formal application required, ED3900, ED 4083
, ED 4085
or ED 4086
with a minimum grade of “B”

records.title: Student Teaching in Middle School and Seminar, Grades (5-9)
records.sourceText:
Credits: 12
This is the capstone student teaching experience for candidates seeking certification in middle childhood education in
biology, chemistry, mathematics, and Spanish. This course provides an opportunity for candidates to apply knowledge
and skills developed in coursework under the guidance of a university supervisor and cooperating teacher. This course
is a full-time commitment, with half the semester spent at grades 5-6 and half at grades 7-9. Students participate in a
weekly seminar.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, formal application required, ED3900, ED 4082
, ED 4083
, ED 4085
or ED 4086
with a minimum grade of “B”

records.title: Teaching Linguistically and Culturally Diverse Students
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
The course is designed to prepare early childhood and elementary teachers to acknowledge and incorporate the valuable
cultural and linguistic resources of the diverse children enrolled in U.S. schools to enrich the schooling experiences of all
children. The course will provide an overview of applied linguistics, theories of second language acquisition, and
culturally sustaining pedagogies. Teacher candidates will employ research-based planning, instruction, and assessment
strategies to meet the needs of English learners and other diverse children enrolled in mainstream classrooms.

When Offered:
Fall
Spring

records.title: Current Topics in Bilingual Education
records.sourceText:
Credits: 2
This course will provide a historical overview of bilingual education in the U.S. as well as exploration of the current
policies and programs for bilingual learners. Time will be dedicated to exploring the bilingual populations as well as
important sub-groups within it including newcomers, SIFE, and bilingual students enrolled in special education
programs. This course will focus on ways that teachers and schools can acknowledge and incorporate the valuable
cultural and linguistic resources of bilingual children, their families and their communities to enrich the schooling
experiences of emerging bilingual children. Field experience required.
Prerequisites
ED3800, ED3900, ED3820, ED4850

records.title: Internship: Meeting the Needs of Diverse Learners
records.sourceText:
Credits: 4
This course is the first of two fieldwork experiences required for Special Education majors in their senior year. The
course provides opportunities for pre-service teachers to apply the knowledge and skills developed in coursework to a
classroom setting that supports children with disabilities. Students are assigned to area schools for 100 hours. Students
are also required to participate in weekly seminar sessions.
Prerequisites
Admission to SOE, ED 3820
, ED 4850, Senior Standing, Approval of SOE program advisor

When Offered:
This course is offered every semester. This course may only be repeated once.

records.title: Student Teaching and Seminar
records.sourceText:
Credits: 12
Student Teaching and Senior Seminar is the final student teaching field experience required of Teacher Education majors.
The course provides opportunity to refine and reflect upon the knowledge, skills, and attitudes needed to become
effective elementary school teachers. Students are assigned to area schools and are required to student teach 5 days a
week for 15 weeks. Students are also required to participate in seminars in certification preparation sessions.
Prerequisites
Completion of all course work and approval of SOE program advisor Grade of “B” or better required
When Offered:
Every semester. This course cannot be repeated

records.title: Student Teaching & Seminar in Diverse Classrooms: Teachers as
records.sourceText:
Leaders/Advocates for All Students and their Families
Credits: 6

Student Teaching is the final student teaching field experience required of Teacher Education majors. The course
provides an opportunity to refine and reflect upon the knowledge, skills, and attitudes needed to become effective
elementary school teachers. Students are assigned to area schools and are required to student teach 5 days a week in two
rotations for a total of 15 weeks within two grade levels (PreK-6 and 7-12). Students are also required to participate in
weekly seminar sessions with the University Field Supervisor. ED 5960 is offered every semester. 70 days of student
teaching experience required.
Prerequisites
Admission to TED; successful completion of ED 5930; approval of TED faculty advisor and Director of Field Experience;
Senior Standing.
ED 5960B - Student Teaching & Seminar - Bilingual
Credits: 6
This is the first half of the final student teaching experience for students seeking dual certification as elementary and
special education teachers. The course provides opportunities for students to refine and reflect upon the knowledge,
skills, and attitudes needed to become effective elementary school teachers. Students are assigned to selected area
schools and required to student teach 5 days a week for 15 weeks. Students are also required to participate in weekly
certification preparation sessions. This course cannot be repeated
Prerequisites
Completion of all course work and approval of program advisor Grade of “B” or better required

records.title: Trends and Issues in High Incidence Disabilities
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course explores current trends, issues and best-practices in working with PreK-12th grade students with high
incidence disabilities. Topics with an emphasis on evidence based strategy instruction, behavioral intervention and
curriculum resources will be addressed. The purpose of this course is to provide pre-service teachers with the skills and
knowledge required for teaching students with high-incidence disabilities (LD, ADHD, EBD, Communication Disorders,
and Mild Intellectual Disabilities) in inclusive settings. Characteristics of students in high-incidence disability categories,
current special education mandates, and trends and issues will be discussed. Students will identify, select, and

demonstrate appropriate teaching strategies, technology, and behavioral support for individuals with high incidence
disabilities in various PreK-12 situations. The is a 15-hour field component is required for this course.

records.title: Methods of Instruction for Students with Low Incidence Disabilities
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course focuses on the characteristics and issues encountered by PreK-12th grade individuals with low incidence dis‐
abilities. Characteristics addressed include learning, behavioral, social-emotional, and communicative abilities. Special
emphasis is placed on implementing evidence-based practices and empirically supported treatments.
Students will identify, select, and demonstrate appropriate teaching strategies, technology, and behavioral support for
individuals with low incidence disabilities in various PreK-12 situations. There is a 15-hour field component is required
for this course.
Prerequisites

records.title: Collaborative Leaders in Special Education
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
Description: This course provides methods of collaboration in PreK-12th grade special and general educational settings.
All aspects of professional collaboration and the interface among general and special educators are highlighted.
Relationships with related service providers as well as parents and external agency personnel are explored with the
focus on PreK-12th grade students with exceptional needs in inclusive settings. Inclusive practices through evidence-
based frameworks are selected with research-based instructional strategies to effectively co-teach in classrooms with
students with diverse needs. There is a 15-hour field component is required for this course.
Prerequisites

, , , , , , and .

records.title: Interventions in Reading for Students with Exceptionalities
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course will review evidence-based strategy instruction to better understand instructional methods and theories to
help PreK-12 students who struggle with literacy to read for understanding and to write for communication of ideas.
Theories of literacy skill development and individual learning styles are examined in the context of various difficulties
encountered in mastering literacy skills. Interventions utilizing a strength-based approach within the framework of the
principles of Universal Design for Learning for all aspects of literacy acquisition are addressed across various PreK-12
settings. There is a 15-hour field component is required for this course.
Prerequisites
ED 7001, ED 7002, ED 7003, ED 7004, ED 7005, and ED 7019

records.title: Math, Science, and Technology for Students with Learning Difficulties
records.sourceText:
Credits: 3
This course provides enhanced application for curriculum development, instructional planning, and validated
instructional strategies for teaching math, science, and technology to PreK-12 students with diverse learning. The uses of
assistive and instructional technology for students with exceptional needs are specifically addressed. Students will
identify, select, and demonstrate appropriate teaching strategies for individuals with exceptionalities in various PreK-12
situations. There is a 15-hour field component is required for this course.
Prerequisites
ED 7001, ED 7002, ED 7003, ED 7004, ED 7005, ED 7019, ED 7021, and ED 7022

records.title: Student Teaching/Final Practicum & Seminar
records.sourceText:
Credits: 6

This course provides a supervised student teaching practicum/research project as the required capstone course for the
degree. The practicum provides the candidates with an opportunity to teach PreK-12th grade learners with
exceptionalities in a school setting under the direction of a cooperating teacher and a college supervisor. For those
students initially certified in special education, an individual research project may be substituted under the direction of
the student’s advisor.
Prerequisites
ED 7001, ED 7002, ED 7003, ED 7004, ED 7005, ED 7019, ED 7020, ED 7021, ED 7022, and ED 7023
